claim: Across the children's-book grid, 66.1% of animal characters are he/him, 31.3% are she/her, and 2.6% are it (the Other category).

source: In the children’s books, male animal characters appeared twice as often as female characters.
claim: The children's-book grid has 556 he/him characters and 263 she/her characters, more than twice as many male as female.

source: After filtering the data to focus on animals who were explicitly gendered (she/her or he/him) and appeared in at least 10 different books, only a few animals were more consistently gendered female: birds, ducks, and cats. The rest—frog, wolf, fox, elephant, dog, monkey, bear, rabbit, mouse, and pig—skew male.
claim: Among animals in at least 10 books, the highest she/her shares of explicitly gendered characters are duck (57.1%), bird (54.3%) and cat (48.1%); every other animal is below 40%: mouse 38.6%, bear 37.9%, pig 37.8%, rabbit 31.9%, dog 19.5%, monkey 17.6%, elephant 16.7%, fox 10.5%, wolf 10.0% and frog 5.9%.

source: Only two percent of the animals were described as it. They/them was almost never used.
claim: The children's-book data contains 22 characters described as it (2.6% of all characters) and no characters described as they/them.

source: In the survey responses to our experiment, no animal tilted more female than male.
claim: For every survey animal, he/him outnumbers she/her among explicitly gendered responses: she/her is 34.4% for cat, 30.2% for bird, 25.8% for pig, 24.1% for rabbit, 23.5% for mouse, 22.4% for dog, and 19.7% for bear.

source: Male pronouns appeared nearly three times as often in the survey results—particularly striking because there were more women respondents.
claim: In the survey data, he appears 529 times and she 178 times, nearly three times as many male pronouns.

source: particularly striking because there were more women respondents
claim: There were more female survey respondents (578) than male respondents (413).

source: While he/him was still the most frequently used pronoun in the survey results, many respondents referred to the animal by name (26%), by it (17%)
claim: In the survey responses, 25.9% have no pronoun (the animal is referred to by name) and 17.3% use it, while he is the most frequent pronoun at 39.9%.

source: Ladybugs are gendered as female in three of the four different books where they appear in our dataset.
claim: In the children's-book data, three ladybug characters are she/her and one is it.

source: While pigs were coded as male for a long time—hello, Three Little Pigs and the Big Bad Wolf—they took a strong feminine turn around the new millennium.
claim: Before 2000, 11 of 35 pig characters (31.4%) are she/her; from 2000 onward, 6 of 10 (60.0%) are she/her.
code: k[k.animal_group=='pig'].assign(period=lambda d: np.where(d.pub_year>=2000,'2000 or later','before 2000')).groupby('period').agg(n=('pronoun','size'), she=('pronoun',lambda x:(x=='she/her').sum())).assign(she_share=lambda d:d.she/d.n)

source: While broad patterns haven’t shifted over time, we did find plenty of meaningful exceptions.
claim: The share of she/her children's-book characters never exceeds 41.1% in any decade category (ranging from 23.9% in the 1950s to 41.1% in the 1990s), so he/him remains the majority throughout.
